title: 3-Read Friday #103: Checking for Understanding, Tutor-Proof Tests, and AI Localisation
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #103 opens with Shaun Brien arguing that checking for understanding is not about gauging confidence or asking if students 'get it,' but about using structured, whole-class strategies like TAPPLE to make thinking visible, catch misconceptions in real time, and inform responsive teaching decisions. Daisy Christodoulou then makes the case that the concept of a 'tutor-proof' selection test is fundamentally flawed, because the practice effect ensures any test format becomes coachable, and replacing curriculum-based assessments with abstract reasoning tasks risks equal social exclusion while promoting less educationally valuable preparation. The issue closes with a paper shared by Barton's colleague Claire, showing that AI models perform significantly worse at contextualising educational content for low- and middle-income countries, with existing benchmarks revealing gaps in cultural accuracy, geographic coverage, and the ability to move beyond stereotypes. Barton frames the AI-localisation paper as a caution for teachers and policymakers to apply careful human review to AI-generated materials in under-represented contexts.
points: Brien's TAPPLE-based framework treats 'checking for understanding' as a structured, whole-class visibility technique, not a vague confidence check -- the goal is catching misconceptions in real time and adjusting teaching immediately.

Christodoulou's tutor-proof-test critique: the practice effect makes any selection-test format coachable, so abstract-reasoning tests don't escape social exclusion, they just trade curriculum-relevant prep for less educationally valuable prep.

The AI-localisation paper found existing benchmarks reveal real gaps in cultural accuracy, geographic coverage, and stereotype avoidance when AI models generate content for low- and middle-income country contexts.

Barton's practical takeaway from the localisation paper: teachers and policymakers in under-represented contexts need to apply careful human review to AI-generated materials, not assume global-benchmark performance transfers.
